odysseyJourney.label: Troy
odysseyJourney.note: Departs for home after ten years at war.
odysseyJourney.connection: The narrative voyage begins on the coast of the Troad after Troy has fallen. Odysseus sails west with twelve ships, expecting a comparatively short return to Ithaca.

odysseyJourney.label: Ismarus
odysseyJourney.note: Raids the Cicones — the first sign the voyage will go wrong.
odysseyJourney.connection: The fleet follows the northern Aegean coast from Troy to the territory of the Cicones. This is the last leg that can be placed on a plausible real-world course with much confidence.

odysseyJourney.label: Lotus-Eaters
odysseyJourney.note: A storm drives the fleet to a land where memory of home dissolves.
odysseyJourney.connection: After leaving Ismarus, Odysseus attempts to round Cape Malea for Ithaca. A north wind drives the ships south for nine days; the line therefore sweeps through the Aegean, below Crete, and west across open water rather than crossing mainland Greece.

odysseyJourney.label: Cyclopes
odysseyJourney.note: Blinds Polyphemus, then makes the fatal mistake of naming himself.
odysseyJourney.connection: The poem gives no bearings between the Lotus-Eaters and the Cyclopes. The reference reconstruction follows the later western-Mediterranean tradition eastward toward Sicily.

odysseyJourney.label: Aeolia
odysseyJourney.note: Given the winds in a bag — opened by his own crew in sight of Ithaca.
odysseyJourney.connection: After escaping Polyphemus, the surviving fleet sails north to the floating island of Aeolus. Its placement near the Aeolian Islands is traditional, not a coordinate supplied by Homer.

odysseyJourney.label: Laestrygonians
odysseyJourney.note: Giant cannibals destroy eleven of twelve ships in one ambush.
odysseyJourney.connection: The winds first carry the fleet almost to Ithaca, but the crew opens Aeolus’s bag and is blown back. After Aeolus refuses further help, the ships sail onward to the enclosed harbour of the Laestrygonians.

odysseyJourney.label: Circe
odysseyJourney.note: Circe turns his men to swine, then becomes his guide to the dead.
odysseyJourney.connection: Only Odysseus’s ship escapes the Laestrygonian harbour. It sails south to Aeaea, where the crew remains with Circe for a year before she directs them toward the dead.

odysseyJourney.label: Land of the Dead
odysseyJourney.mapPlacement: Diagrammatic western Mediterranean, following the reference map
odysseyJourney.note: At the edge of the world, consults the prophet Tiresias.
odysseyJourney.connection: Circe instructs Odysseus to cross Ocean to a land of darkness at the world’s edge. The north-western placement follows the supplied narrative map; it is a diagrammatic location, not an archaeological claim.

odysseyJourney.label: Sirens
odysseyJourney.note: Returns to Circe, then hears the Sirens while bound to his own mast.
odysseyJourney.connection: After speaking with Tiresias, Odysseus returns to Circe to bury Elpenor and receive detailed sailing instructions. Only then does he pass the Sirens, so the line deliberately returns to Aeaea before continuing south.

odysseyJourney.label: Scylla & Charybdis
odysseyJourney.note: Chooses a certain small loss over a possible total one.
odysseyJourney.connection: The Sirens are followed immediately by the Wandering Rocks and the narrow passage between Scylla and Charybdis. The traditional map carries the ship south along the Italian coast toward the Strait of Messina.

odysseyJourney.label: Cattle of the Sun
odysseyJourney.note: The crew's hunger overrides two warnings — with fatal cost.
odysseyJourney.connection: Once through the strait, the crew lands on Thrinacia despite the warnings of both Tiresias and Circe. The reference tradition places the island close to Sicily.

odysseyJourney.label: Calypso
odysseyJourney.mapPlacement: Diagrammatic south-west of Sicily, following the reference map
odysseyJourney.note: Held by Calypso for seven years, offered immortality, wants only home.
odysseyJourney.connection: Zeus destroys the ship after the cattle are killed. Odysseus alone survives, drifting back past Charybdis and then across the sea until he reaches Calypso’s island.

odysseyJourney.label: Phaeacia
odysseyJourney.note: Found naked on a beach by Nausicaa; finally tells his whole story.
odysseyJourney.connection: After seven years, Calypso releases Odysseus on a raft. Poseidon wrecks it, but he swims ashore among the Phaeacians; the sweeping eastern leg represents this final solitary crossing.

odysseyJourney.label: Ithaca
odysseyJourney.note: Returns in disguise and kills the suitors besieging his house.
odysseyJourney.connection: The Phaeacians carry the sleeping Odysseus home in one of their ships and leave him on Ithaca with his gifts. This final leg is short and geographically intelligible, unlike most of the fantastic wanderings.

alexanderJourney.label: Pella
alexanderJourney.control: The opening shaded area represents Macedon and the League of Corinth. The league was a Macedonian-led alliance rather than a uniformly administered annexation, so the map treats the two as related but distinct forms of power.
alexanderJourney.note: 336 BC — becomes king of Macedon at twenty.
alexanderJourney.connection: The campaign begins with the kingdom and army built by Philip II. Alexander first has to secure his succession and reassert Macedonian leadership in Greece before he can cross into Asia.

alexanderJourney.label: Troy
alexanderJourney.control: No major Asian territory is shaded yet. Macedonian power still rests on its European base and fleet crossings; the western Anatolian satrapies remain under Achaemenid authority.
alexanderJourney.note: 334 BC — crosses into Asia and honours Achilles at Troy.
alexanderJourney.connection: Alexander crosses the Hellespont with the invasion army and visits the traditional tomb of Achilles before confronting Persian forces. This is a symbolic and logistical threshold rather than a territorial conquest.

alexanderJourney.label: Granicus
alexanderJourney.control: Anatolia now appears progressively. The polygon is a schematic summary of the campaigning and submissions that followed during 334 BC, not a claim that every district changed hands at the instant of the battle.
alexanderJourney.note: 334 BC — wins his first battle against Persian forces in Asia.
alexanderJourney.connection: From the Troad the army moves north-east to the Granicus, where Alexander attacks the satrapal cavalry at the river crossing. The victory opens the western approaches into Asia Minor.

alexanderJourney.label: Issus
alexanderJourney.control: The victory consolidates the Anatolian campaign and removes the Persian field army from the western theatre. The Levantine coast is not yet secure: Tyre, Gaza and other naval bases still have to be taken.
alexanderJourney.note: 333 BC — defeats Darius III in person on the Cilician coast.
alexanderJourney.connection: Alexander campaigns through Anatolia before turning through the Cilician Gates. Darius moves behind him, forcing the battle onto the narrow coastal plain at Issus.

alexanderJourney.label: Tyre
alexanderJourney.control: The Levantine corridor is added. Phoenician and Cypriot naval contingents change sides as their cities submit, sharply reducing Persian power at sea while securing Alexander’s communications behind him.
alexanderJourney.note: 332 BC — takes the island city after a seven-month siege.
alexanderJourney.connection: Rather than pursue Darius inland immediately, Alexander turns south to eliminate Persian naval bases. Tyre’s refusal forces the longest and most technically demanding siege of the campaign.

alexanderJourney.label: Alexandria
alexanderJourney.control: Egypt appears as a separate stage because its conquest changed both the scale and character of the kingdom. Alexander retained much of the existing administration and adopted pharaonic kingship rather than governing Egypt as if it were simply another Macedonian district.
alexanderJourney.note: 331 BC — founds Alexandria after Egypt accepts his rule.
alexanderJourney.connection: After Tyre and Gaza, Alexander enters Egypt, where Achaemenid rule is unpopular and organized resistance is limited. He founds Alexandria and visits the oracle of Ammon before marching back towards Asia.

alexanderJourney.label: Gaugamela
alexanderJourney.control: Mesopotamia begins to fill in as the route reaches Gaugamela. The victory makes the surrender of Babylon and Susa possible, but Darius remains alive and the Persian heartland has not yet been secured.
alexanderJourney.note: 331 BC — breaks the main Achaemenid army near Gaugamela.
alexanderJourney.connection: Alexander returns through the Levant, crosses the Euphrates and Tigris, and meets Darius on ground prepared for Persian chariots and cavalry. His victory destroys the last great field army defending the imperial capitals.

alexanderJourney.label: Babylon
alexanderJourney.control: This stage represents consolidation rather than a new colour block. Alexander keeps Mazaeus in office and works through Achaemenid institutions, illustrating that control expanded through negotiated submission as well as battlefield victory.
alexanderJourney.note: 331 BC — enters Babylon peacefully as the new king.
alexanderJourney.connection: After Gaugamela, Alexander moves south into Babylon. The city and its satrap Mazaeus surrender without a siege, giving him a major administrative and ceremonial centre.

alexanderJourney.label: Persepolis
alexanderJourney.control: Persia now appears on the map. Alexander can claim the position of Great King, but control remains incomplete while Darius and then Bessus draw resistance eastwards into Iran, Bactria and Sogdiana.
alexanderJourney.note: 330 BC — captures and later burns the Achaemenid ceremonial capital.
alexanderJourney.connection: From Babylon the army takes Susa, crosses the Zagros and enters the Persian heartland. Persepolis yields an enormous treasury and becomes the symbolic end of the Achaemenid court.

alexanderJourney.label: Hydaspes
alexanderJourney.control: Bactria and Sogdiana appear during the first part of this animated leg, followed by the Indus region near its end. Porus is restored as a subordinate ruler, showing that the far east was held through satrapies, garrisons and local dynasts rather than direct uniform government.
alexanderJourney.note: 326 BC — defeats Porus and his war elephants in the Punjab.
alexanderJourney.connection: The long eastern leg represents years of difficult campaigning through Iran, Bactria and Sogdiana, then across the Hindu Kush into the Punjab. At the Hydaspes Alexander wins his last major battle; at the Hyphasis his army refuses to continue.

alexanderJourney.label: Babylon
alexanderJourney.control: The final view shows the maximum claimed extent at his death. It was not a homogeneous nation-state: authority varied between Macedonian garrisons, inherited satrapal administrations, allied rulers and recently subdued regions, and it fragmented almost immediately without him.
alexanderJourney.note: 323 BC — returns to Babylon and dies aged thirty-two.
alexanderJourney.connection: The return runs down the Indus and west through Gedrosia, where the desert crossing causes severe losses, before passing through Persia to Babylon. Alexander dies while planning further campaigns.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Egypt
alexanderFoundations.note: Founded on the Mediterranean coast in 331 BC; the best-attested and most consequential of Alexander’s named foundations.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Ariana
alexanderFoundations.note: Usually associated with Herat. Ancient geographers preserve the name, but archaeological confirmation of the identification is lacking.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Arachosia
alexanderFoundations.note: Commonly placed at Old Kandahar, probably as a refoundation or garrison settlement on an existing Achaemenid centre.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria Prophthasia
alexanderFoundations.note: The Drangian capital Phrada, renamed after Alexander uncovered Philotas's conspiracy there in October 330 BC. Usually placed at modern Farah, Afghanistan, though the identification rests on tradition rather than confirmed excavation.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria of the Caucasus
alexanderFoundations.note: The foundation is reported in the campaign tradition, but its exact site north of Kabul remains disputed; the marker uses the Bagram area.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria Eschate
alexanderFoundations.note: The “Furthest Alexandria,” built as a fortified outpost on the Jaxartes near modern Khujand.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria on the Oxus
alexanderFoundations.note: Often linked with Ai-Khanoum, although both that identification and an Alexandrian rather than Seleucid foundation remain disputed.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Margiana
alexanderFoundations.note: Associated with the Merv oasis and later refounded as Antioch; the surviving foundation tradition is not archaeologically decisive.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria Bucephala
alexanderFoundations.note: Founded on the west bank of the Hydaspes in May 326 BC in memory of Alexander's horse Bucephalus, who died there. Proposed sites near modern Jhelum, Pakistan (Phalia, Jalalpur Sharif, Garjak) remain debated.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria Nicaea
alexanderFoundations.note: Founded opposite Bucephala on the east bank of the Hydaspes at the same time, commemorating the victory over Porus ("Nicaea" — city of victory). Often placed near modern Mong, though the site is disputed.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria on the Indus
alexanderFoundations.note: Placed schematically near the Indus–Acesines confluence. A city foundation is reported, but its precise location and later name are uncertain.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria among the Oritai
alexanderFoundations.note: Alexander ordered a city founded at Rhambacia on the return journey; its later identification as an Alexandria is less secure.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Carmania
alexanderFoundations.note: A later geographical tradition places an Alexandria in Carmania, but ancient testimony and the proposed site remain uncertain.

alexanderFoundations.name: Alexandria in Susiana
alexanderFoundations.note: Founded in 324 BC near the confluence of the Tigris and Karun at the head of the Persian Gulf; later refounded as Antioch-in-Susiana and then Charax Spasinou. Archaeologists identified the site, near modern Basra, Iraq.
